newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end barely changed.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end barely changed.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices ended barely changed on Friday after profit-taking in front of new supply erased early gains.
The market opened higher after a recovery in European bond prices overnight spurred buying in London.

The gains were soon abetted by news that the U.S. trade deficit in goods and services shrank to $10.83 billion in August from a revised $11.60 billion July gap, much wider than the $8.5 billion deficit economists had anticipated.
The deterioration in U.S. net exports offered further evidence of weak third-quarter economic growth, prompting economists to trim their third-quarter GDP (gross domestic product) forecasts.

Elliott Platt, managing director, economic research, at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette, said the trade data prompted him to cut his third-quarter GDP forecast to 1.4 percent from his previously estimated 1.7 percent.
"The market advanced because the trade deficit indicated that the economy was even weaker than previously thought," said Platt.

"The market has been busy pricing in signs that the economy is slowing," said Josh Stiles, senior bond strategist at I.D.E.A. "The most significant event on Friday was the wider-than-expected trade deficit coming just a day after signs of slowing in housing and manufacturing."
The government reported on Thursday that new housing starts fell six percent in September and the Federal Reserve said industrial production rose just 0.2 percent in September.
But while the conviction grows that the Fed will not tighten its grip on interest rates this year -- supporting the market -- profit-taking emerged late in the session.

"There was obviously a motivated seller, and contrary to conventional market wisdom, price changes that take place in a thinly traded market do stick," said Chris Rupkey, vice president and economist at Bank of Tokyo/Mitsubishi.
Rupkey said the market's retreat from the 6.75 percent level on the 30-year bond yield marked the third time that the yield had approached that level and backed away from it.
The 6-3/4 percent 30-year benchmark Treasury bond ended at 99-12/32, up 1/32, to yield 6.80 percent.
"We're left near the top of the six-month trading range," said Stiles.
Analysts said concern about upcoming supply next week might have played a role in the market's late downturn.
The Treasury will sell $18.25 billion in two-year notes on Tuesday and $12.5 billion in five-year notes on Wednesday.
At the short end of the maturity curve, three- and six-month bill rates rose three basis points to 4.98 percent and 5.09 percent, respectively. Year-bill rates rose two basis points to 5.23 percent.

The two-year note ended at 100-7/32, down 1/32, to yield 5.88 percent. Five-year notes ended at 100-17/32, down 1/32, to yield 6.25 percent. The ten-year note closed unchanged at 99-31/32 to yield 6.50 percent. -- 212-859-1679
